item.title: Dolly Parton’s sister reveals ‘last thing’ country legend asked of her before death
item.description: Stella Parton said that prayer was the last thing Dolly Parton asked for before her death from a brief battle with cancer.
item.content:encoded:
Dolly Parton's sister is sharing the final request she received from the musician.

During a recent interview with "CBS Mornings," Stella Parton shared the last thing her sister asked of her before her death.

"That’s the last thing Dolly asked me for, was prayer," she recalled.

The legendary musician died on Tuesday, Aug. 25 at the age of 80, following a "brief battle with cancer," which she hid from her fans, and even some family members.

DOLLY PARTON OFFERED TO TRY EXPERIMENTAL DRUGS IF ‘NO HOPE’ FOR CANCER BATTLE TO HELP OTHERS, SISTER SAYS

Stella noted that the family will not be sharing what type of cancer Dolly had "out of respect for her" since Dolly "didn't tell us that we could say it," adding that she is able to speak about her love for her sister, but when it comes to her health, "it's not my business to tell her business."

Concerns over the "Jolene" singer's health first arose in September 2025, when she made the difficult decision to postpone a number of shows in Las Vegas, Nevada, telling fans she needed to undergo a "few procedures."

"I want the fans and public to hear directly from me that, unfortunately, I will need to postpone my upcoming Las Vegas concerts," Parton shared online at the time. "As many of you know, I have been dealing with some health challenges, and my doctors tell me that I must have a few procedures."

Shortly after Dolly made her announcement, concern among fans increased when her sister Freida asked fans to pray for Dolly, saying, "Many of you know she hasn’t been feeling her best lately."

When speaking with "CBS Mornings," Stella noted, "I think Dolly got on to Freida about that."

DOLLY PARTON’S ONGOING HEALTH BATTLE FORCES COUNTRY LEGEND TO MISS MAJOR DOLLYWOOD EVENT

"I'm pretty sure Dolly said, 'You're going to, you know, pipe it down,' because that was the first time people thought 'oh,'" she said. "And she knew that Freida was just upset and hurt, but she thought, 'Don't be telling my situation, Freida. Don't be spilling my business.'"

According to Stella, Dolly decided to keep her diagnosis a secret because she "could not bear negative things" and didn't want her fans to worry about her.

Her death came a little over a year after the death of her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean, who died in March 2025 at the age of 82. While some have speculated Dolly died of a broken heart, Stella doesn't agree.

"I think she was very sad, but I don't think that's why she got sick," Stella said. "I think she worked too hard and didn't maybe take as good a care of herself as she should have. She at one point, she said, 'You know, I spent a lot of time caring for Carl that maybe I neglected myself.'"

DOLLY PARTON LAID TO REST AS NIECE SHARES EMOTIONAL TRIBUTE TO ‘GRANNY’

She went on to say that while it "broke her heart to see him in the shape he" was in before he died, she ultimately believes Dolly's determination to continue working "so hard for so long" contributed to her passing.

When speaking about Dolly's relationship with Dean, she referred to it as "very unique and very deep and loyal," and gave Dean credit for being supportive of Dolly and loving "her enough to let her be what she was."

Stella explained that while Dolly was a huge star across the globe, Dean "didn't care about that at all," and if it was up to him, she would have been "at the house with her hair up in a ponytail and barefooted cooking in the kitchen." Stella said even family members rarely saw Dolly without her signature glamorous look after she became a star.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Not after she got to be Dolly Parton. No. She would sleep in her makeup when she'd come spend the night with me," Stella said. "Oh, I knew what she looked like. She looked like me without her makeup. So, I knew what she looked like without it."

Her sister also credited Dolly for being a good businesswoman, saying that while she had opinions on politics and other controversial topics, she never shared them because "she would never have offended anyone."

Although Dolly was battling cancer, Stella says she knows her sister was at peace in her final moments.

"She knew where she was going," she said. "She wasn't going anywhere bad. She was going to be with mom and daddy. She was prepared. Yeah, she was definitely prepared."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

When it comes to how she hopes her sister is remembered, Stella said she wants people to think of her as "very sweet, kind, loving, brilliant and so talented."

"Her creativity had no bounds, and she could dream bigger than anybody," Stella said. "And I want young people, young girls and boys that may think they have no opportunity to dream. Coming from our situation, she gave us permission to dream that way."

item.title: Nike shareholders reject transparency proposal as faith-based firm questions DEI commitments
item.description: Tim Schwarzenberger explains why Nike's perfect Human Rights Campaign score and DEI ties sparked a shareholder proposal at its annual meeting.
item.content:encoded:
Tim Schwarzenberger’s last pair of Nike sneakers is about 10 years old and the shoes have holes in them.

But the Christian investor who helped lead a shareholder campaign demanding more transparency from Nike says he wants a reason to buy another pair.

"For me, what resonates is forgiveness," Schwarzenberger told OutKick. "If companies make changes, we need to applaud them."

NIKE FORGOT THAT REPUBLICANS BUY SNEAKERS, TOO, AND NOW IT'S GETTING BOOTED FROM THE S&P 100

"I would like to get back to buying the shoes, but I can’t rationalize doing that when Nike has become so activist," he said. "If the company can change, I would be the first to applaud them and get in line."

Schwarzenberger is a portfolio manager and director of corporate engagement at Inspire Investing, a faith-based firm that represents investors who own Nike stock. Those investors make money if Nike succeeds, not if it collapses.

"We’re long-term investors," he said. "Our primary goal is to earn competitive performance for the investors we serve, and we want companies to do well."

Nike shareholders rejected Proposal 5 during the company’s annual meeting Sept. 8. Inspire backed the proposal on behalf of client William C. Cunningham.

The resolution asked Nike to evaluate and issue a report analyzing the "benefits, costs, and legal, reputational, competitive, and other relevant risks" associated with its charitable support.

The proposal’s supporting statement specifically cited Nike’s verified score of 100 on the Human Rights Campaign’s Corporate Equality Index. Inspire argued that the score raises questions about whether Nike’s employee health plan covers gender-transition procedures for minors, including surgery, cross-sex hormone therapy, menstruation suppression and puberty blockers.

Schwarzenberger said Nike has not publicly answered whether it provides those benefits to minor dependents.

HRC's 2026 criteria require transgender-inclusive health benefits for full credit, but Nike's public HRC profile does not disclose the company's age limits or dependent-specific plan terms.

The proposal also pointed to Nike’s broader DEI initiatives and argued that its charitable relationships with advocacy organizations could create legal, reputational and financial risks.

Nike’s board recommended that shareholders reject the proposal, arguing in its 2026 proxy statement that the company already evaluates those risks.

"The company’s current approach to charitable giving, together with our existing disclosures and guidelines, appropriately serves the best interests of our shareholders," Nike stated.

The company also said creating another report would consume time and resources without providing additional value to investors.

Detailed vote totals were not yet available when OutKick interviewed Schwarzenberger. Nike disclosed the results in a September 10 SEC filing, showing the proposal received less than 1% of votes cast for or against it.

"Most shareholder proposals do not receive majority support, so that was not a surprise," Schwarzenberger said. "But we were able to make the case to shareholders and raise issues that I think are on the minds of many shareholders."

Nike said charitable partnerships are approved only after what it described as a "robust due diligence review."

"Any time I hear the word robust, it kind of scares me," Schwarzenberger said. "Are they actually concerned about the end investor?"

Proposal 5 focused heavily on Nike’s relationship with the Human Rights Campaign and its Corporate Equality Index, which evaluates companies on their LGBTQ workplace policies and practices.

Nike received a verified score of 100 on the 2026 Corporate Equality Index. The Human Rights Campaign recognizes companies receiving that score as leaders in LGBTQ workplace inclusion.

Schwarzenberger said the score means Nike is complying with what Inspire considers an increasingly left-wing set of corporate requirements.

"They’re doing all the things that the Human Rights Campaign has asked for," he said. "It’s really been like a moving treadmill where they’ve upped the ante every single version. The goalposts are always switching."

Participation in the survey declined sharply this year. According to HRC’s own report, the number of Fortune 500 companies submitting information fell 65%, from 377 companies in 2025 to 131 in 2026.

HRC said the decrease in public reporting does not necessarily mean the companies changed their underlying workplace policies.

Nike remained a participant.

Schwarzenberger argued that Nike’s continued participation in HRC’s Corporate Equality Index raises questions about whether the company has adequately considered the legal, reputational and financial risks of its partnerships.

"Our ask is simply to provide transparency into what Nike is doing," he said. "If the company has analyzed the risk of these organizations, then let us see it."

"Nike is set to be removed from the S&P 100 before trading begins Sept. 21, after nearly 18 years in the blue-chip index.

S&P Dow Jones Indices said the rebalance is intended to make its indexes more representative of their market-cap ranges.

The company’s market cap has fallen by more than $200 billion since its November 2021 peak. Nike has also lost ground to newer competitors and faced product challenges, while Greater China revenue fell 13% on a currency-neutral basis in fiscal 2026.

TED CRUZ TAKES VICTORY LAP AS ICONIC AMERICAN BRAND'S STOCK PLUNGES TO 12-YEAR LOW

Schwarzenberger acknowledged that Nike’s political decisions cannot be blamed for all of that.

"It is hard to dissect exactly what is causing the share-price decline," he said. "There are many factors, including China and perhaps some missteps with the company’s approach there and with various campaigns."

Still, he believes Nike has made its recovery more difficult by taking positions that anger some potential customers.

"At the very least, don’t do things that are going to upset your customers further," Schwarzenberger said. "If you are alienating half of your customer base, it is difficult to quantify exactly what percentage of the share-price decline is caused by those activities. But it is certainly a distraction."

OutKick has previously detailed Nike’s history with Colin Kaepernick, the canceled Betsy Ross sneaker, Dylan Mulvaney and a proposed study involving transgender youth athletes.

Schwarzenberger said Nike does not need to move toward conservative politics to correct course.

It just needs to stop making politics part of the product at all.

"The company does not need to take sides," he said. "It does not need to go right or left. It needs to stay in the middle, focus on its business and acknowledge its mistakes."

Schwarzenberger said Nike CEO Elliott Hill’s comments about refocusing on athletes were encouraging, but not strong enough to convince him that the company was committed to changing course.

"The CEO’s statement at the annual shareholders meeting about focusing on the athlete was good, but it was kind of a lukewarm response," he said. "They really need to take a very strong approach and say, ‘Look, we’re going to focus on manufacturing athletic apparel, and that’s going to be our focus. We’re not going to wade into hot-button political issues.’"

He also wants Nike to produce better products.

"If Nike does that and begins showing innovation in its products, that would be progress," he said. "Nike should get back to focusing on its core business and show that it is not an advocacy organization. It is an apparel company."

Schwarzenberger compared Nike’s lack of product innovation to Disney’s reliance on brands from the 1990s.

"It’s kind of like Disney. When’s the last time you’ve seen a good Disney movie?" he said. "We’d like to see some innovation."

Schwarzenberger said Inspire filed dozens of shareholder resolutions last year, and roughly two-thirds of the targeted companies made the changes the firm requested.

"The point I would make to conservative investors is that you have a voice," Schwarzenberger said. "For far too long, we have delegated that voice to others who are doing things completely contrary to our values."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

That leverage is not limited to professional investors. Millions of Americans own shares in major companies indirectly through mutual funds held in their 401(k) accounts. Fund managers generally determine how those shares are voted in corporate elections.

Schwarzenberger said workers can review how their fund managers vote and ask their employers or plan administrators to offer additional investment options.

"You have a tremendous voice and a responsibility," he said. "If we show up and start pressuring these companies to get back to business, I think we can see even more success than we have seen so far."

item.title: Fatwas, holy wars and socialism: Inside the Islamic conference where El-Sayed drew a hero’s welcome
item.description: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed headlined an ISNA conference where an attendee called for a fatwa against members of Congress.
item.content:encoded:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed headlined an Islamic conference over Labor Day weekend where the United States was described as an empire in decline, early Islamic conquests were praised and the aftermath of 9/11 was framed around Islamophobia and discrimination.

The event, held annually by the Islamic Society of North America, featured a range of speakers discussing topics from Muslim civic participation to the ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas. Over the course of the conference’s speeches and panel discussions, participants took positions that were generally critical of the United States and the broader Western world and expressed opinions that some may regard as extreme.

Fox News Digital attended the event over the weekend, sitting in on many of the panels held on Saturday and Sunday before and after El-Sayed's speech. The Michigan Democrat is running in one of the most hotly contested Senate races of the 2026 cycle, the outcome of which may decide control of the Senate.

At one panel dubbed "Rising Islamophobia in the U.S.," a speaker described recently passed legislation that could bar colleges participating in certain commercial boycotts of Israel from receiving some federal higher-education funds as "an anti-Muslim bill."

EXILED MUSLIM SCHOLAR WARNS FAR-LEFT–ISLAMIST ALLIANCE BEHIND ANTI-ISRAEL PROTESTS ECHOES IRAN’S RISE

Shortly after that, a man in the audience wearing a Pakistani flag pin stood up and called for a fatwa to be issued against the bipartisan group of lawmakers who voted for the bil. A fatwa is a religious ruling or opinion that can range from a formal condemnation to, in some cases, a call for or justification of violence.

The legislation was introduced by Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., and co-sponsored by Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.

After the man called for a fatwa against members of Congress, members of the audience — and one panelist — applauded.

Earlier during the same discussion, a panelist criticized Congress for moving to censure Reps. Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib for making "​​the most lighthearted comments"

Tlaib was censured in part for endorsing the phrase "from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free" — which calls for the destruction of Israel as bounded by the Jordan River in the east and the Mediterranean Sea in the west. Critics characterized the phrase as a call for ethnic cleansing while the congresswoman defended it as "an aspirational call for freedom, human rights and peaceful coexistence."

ISNA is a nonprofit Muslim religious organization established in 1981 to provide America's growing Muslim population with a platform for civic coordination and education. Detroit, where the event took place, is situated in a metropolitan area that has a significant Arab American population concentrated in areas such as Dearborn and Hamtramck.

EL-SAYED CAMPAIGN BACKED BY OVER $100,000 FROM DOZENS OF MEMBERS OF GROUP WITH ALLEGED TERROR TIES

Panelists also accused billionaire Elon Musk of funding a white supremacist global anti-Muslim movement, suggested that some of the narrative regarding 9/11 taught in American schools has been "debunked," and asserted that Muslims were treated unfairly in the wake of the 2001 attacks.

Criticism of America’s response to 9/11 surfaced repeatedly across the conference’s events and breakout sessions. One speaker asserted that one of the most important things to reflect on as the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approaches is that "Islamophobia is at an all-time high." Another called the War on Terror, a series of post-9/11 military operations that claimed the lives of over 7,000 U.S. military personnel, the "War of Terror."

El-Sayed has sought to moderate his public image since launching his Senate campaign, even as he has maintained ties to prominent socialists and socialist-aligned activists. His attendance at the recent ISNA conference is the latest in a series of associations that have drawn criticism, including ties to Nation of Islam figures, Muslim clerics accused of expressing support for terrorist organizations and activists on the socialist left.

In response to these charges, the Democrat has pointed out that the GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers himself has links to individuals who echo conspiracy theories about the 2020 election or who have called for bans on gay marriage.

EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS

Before the event, El-Sayed’s campaign moved to distance the candidate from other conference speakers.

"Abdul is not affiliated with and does not endorse any other participant of the conference," a spokeswoman for his campaign told media outlets in the lead up to the event.

The statement followed reports that he would appear alongside Islamic clerics who defended child marriage and praised U.S.-designated terrorist organizations, including al Qaeda. Of the controversial speakers, only the cleric who had defended child marriage was ultimately disinvited, the Washington Free Beacon previously reported.

ISNA appeared to anticipate scrutiny over some of the speakers it invited to the conference. In the conference venue’s main hallway, the organization posted a prominent sign which read "ISNA does not endorse the actions of convention participants and explicitly disclaims any responsibility for the views expressed, information provided, or materials displayed, sold or distributed by convention speakers, performers, exhibitors, vendors, or attendees."

COUNTERTERRORISM EXPERT WARNS ABDUL EL-SAYED SENATE BID RAISES HOMELAND SECURITY CONCERNS

While ISNA sought to distance itself from the controversial views expressed by some conference speakers, the organization itself took actions that also drew scrutiny.

Fox News Digital spoke to three Christian evangelists outside the conference who claimed they were removed from it without warning. Each of them said they were simply having conversations with individuals who wanted to speak with them before they were escorted outside by security.

Attendance at the conference was open to people of all faiths, and registration did not require attendees to be Muslim. The conference also held an interfaith banquet on Sunday.

The disclaimer took on added significance in light of books available for purchase at the conference’s on-site bazaar. Fox News Digital found books that defended Islamic warfare while portraying Christianity as uniquely violent.

"Christians are the last people on earth who should bring the charge of bloodshed and cruelty against followers of any other system, for it is a well-established fact that no religion known to history has such a horrible sanguinary record as church Christianity," one book sold at the conference reads.

Another book argued that all Islamic warfare is defensive, defended non-Muslims being forced to pay a discriminatory tax and claimed that Christian civilization has killed nearly 200 million people by attributing wars that did not have religious motivations or were not initiated by Christians. The French Revolution, which was instigated by individuals hostile to Christianity, for instance, is counted toward Christianity’s death count. The Korean War, which was launched by communist North Korea, is also counted toward the body count of Christianity.

UNEARTHED INTERVIEW REVEALS EL-SAYED’S SHARIA ‘OBLIGATION’: ‘NOT BECAUSE OF FEAR’

The conference also featured advertisements for "Sharia-compliant" mortgages and other financial products.

El-Sayed held a quasi-celebrity status among the conference’s attendees. Campaign buttons were nearly ubiquitous at the conference and his campaign’s booth was easily the busiest of those located in the main hall, Fox News Digital found.

When the Senate hopeful walked onto stage to address the conference, he was greeted with a thunderous standing ovation. Calls of "we love you" rang out from the crowd.

El-Sayed’s speech was ultimately measured and largely focused on unity, representation and the idea that Muslim and American identities are compatible.

"As we leave here tonight, I’ve got a challenge for each and every one of you," El-Sayed said with a measured cadence reminiscent of former President Barack Obama. "It’s the question of how you show up in the spaces in which you show up everyday, as wholly and 100% yourself. Because we are a community as Muslim Americans who believe in the rhyming of our Muslim ideals and our American ideals. That those two things are not mutually exclusive, in fact, that at their best being Muslim makes us better Americans and being Muslim enables us to be better Americans."

‘DESTROYING THE AMERICAN WAY OF LIFE’: EL-SAYED’S POLITICAL ORBIT COMPLICATES EFFORT TO MODERATE HIS IMAGE

But elsewhere at the conference, speakers offered a markedly different assessment of America and its place in the world.

"The world has become multipolar and we see almost like the fear and insecurity that the empire has at this moment. If we think through the lens of the U.S. So I like to think that we are on the very end of an ending empire," an academic speaking at a session about the conflict between Israel and Hamas said. "I'm very positive about it."

The same panelist later argued that referring to the river next to Detroit as the "Detroit River" was an immoral act of colonialism because Native Americans had a different name for the waterway.

In a similar vein, a speaker at one of the conference’s main sessions criticized American foreign policy following the 9/11 terrorist attacks, then credited the "TikTok generation" with mobilizing in favor of Palestinians following the Oct. 7 terrorist attacks.

Some speakers, however, made a clear effort to connect El-Sayed’s socialist project with his Islamic faith.

"Islam historically was not just spread by the instance of Dawah, it was spread by socialism," a cleric who would go on to speak positively about early Islamic conquests, said.

ISNA declined comment. The El-Sayed campaign did not respond to requests for comment after being reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

item.title: 4 shot inside North Carolina home, 2 killed as police identify person of interest
item.description: Authorities said two victims died at the home, and two others were hospitalized with life-threatening injuries after the shooting in Gaston County, North Carolina.
item.content:encoded:
A shooting inside a Gaston County, North Carolina, home left two people dead and two others critically injured Thursday morning after police responded to a 911 call reporting gunfire, authorities said.

The Gaston County Police Department said officers responded to the house just before 8:45 a.m. and found four victims inside with gunshot wounds.

Two of the victims were pronounced dead at the home, while the remaining two were taken to a nearby hospital with life-threatening injuries, police said.

3 DEAD, INCLUDING SUSPECTED GUNMAN, AND 3 OFFICERS INJURED IN MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING

A person of interest has been identified in the shooting, but police did not reveal additional information. 

Investigators believe the suspect and victims knew each other and that the shooting was an isolated incident.

NORTH CAROLINA WOMAN CHARGED IN ALLEGED HOUSTON SYNAGOGUE ATTACK PLOT AS INVESTIGATORS SEARCH FOR 2 OTHERS

Authorities said they are continuing to investigate the circumstances.

There is no known ongoing threat to the Gaston County community, police said.

Gaston County is roughly 30 minutes west of Charlotte and just north of the South Carolina border.

Anyone with additional information is asked to call the Gaston County Police Department at 704-866-3320 or CrimeStoppers at 704-861-8000.

item.title: Suzy Kolber opens up about ESPN firing, emotional reaction: 'I lost it'
item.description: Suzy Kolber revealed the emotional phone call and non-disparagement clause that followed her ESPN layoff after 27 years hosting "Monday Night Countdown."
item.content:encoded:
Suzy Kolber was part of a 20-talent layoff at ESPN in June 2023, along with Steve Young, Max Kellerman and Jalen Rose. At the time, Kolber hosted the network’s "Monday Night Countdown" pregame show.

Kolber spoke about her firing for the first time during a conversation on the "Sports Media with Richard Deitsch" podcast this week.

"He [ESPN president Jimmy Pitaro] said, ‘Suzy there’s a whiteboard and your name’s on it. I don’t really know for sure right now but your name is on it,'" she said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

It’s unclear how the head of the company didn’t know whether Kolber was safe. Nonetheless, she recalled coming home that night and having a conversation with her daughter.

"I remember that day sitting next to my daughter in the kitchen. For years I’ve said ‘You never know.’ And I sat down next to her and I cried. And I said, ‘I think this is really happening.’"

The following week, Kolber received a call from then-ESPN executive Norby Williamson, best known as a supporter of Mark Jones.

Kolber said she "lost it" when Williamson told her she couldn’t say "anything disparaging about the company or we can take the last year of your contract."

Before her layoff, Kolber had agreed to take a pay cut.

"I did think the 39% cut was going to get me to the end [of my career]," she said.

Perhaps Kolber should have remained silent about her firing. She didn’t help herself with these comments.

For one, she comes off as entitled. We understand that a layoff can be emotional, regardless of the circumstances. However, a non-disparagement provision is standard. Kolber is no different from any other talent laid off with time remaining on their contract.

There was hardly a reason to "lose it," as she put it, over the clause.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Kolber also worked at ESPN for 27 years. She is now 62. She hosted the network’s top pregame show. ESPN didn’t owe her anything else. And yet, she suggested that she was unhappy with the lack of appreciation she received during her departure.

"I just thought after 27 years of, I was the first person hired for the launch of ESPN 2. I was the first person assigned to the X Games," she continued. "I went and shot the marketing tape for it. ‘Monday Night Football’s’ move to ESPN, I was part of some pretty big franchises. You’re not going to say a word? Not thanks for 27 years, just acknowledge it? I didn’t understand that."

At least her bosses didn’t fire her on-air, mid-show, as they did Ryan Clark in an apparent attempt to spite OutKick.

Our understanding is that Kolber’s firing was about the numbers. The network needed to shed a certain amount of talent salary, and she became expendable because ESPN employed other anchors who could fill her role. ESPN eventually tapped Scott Van Pelt to replace Kolber on "Countdown."

ESPN likely would have made a change at the position regardless, with its first-ever Super Bowl broadcast coming this fall. The anchor of "Monday Night Countdown" will also host the Super Bowl and its halftime show.

As one of the faces of the network, Van Pelt was a favorite for the position before 2023.

The network arguably has more NFL hosts than it has major sports. Van Pelt hosts Mondays. Mike Greenberg hosts the Sunday morning pregame show. Laura Rutledge, the host of "NFL Live," would be the lead football anchor at most networks and arguably should be at ESPN.

Therefore, Kolber became the odd person out.

Still, Kolber was a good host. Her talent and production were not the issues. In fact, since executive Burke Magnus is in the business of rehiring previous anchors, he should have brought her back.

Instead — in what appears to be a make-good for firing Ryan Clark — Magnus rehired Stan Verrett, who has a weird obsession with OutKick and race talk, to anchor a show on NFL Network.

Kolber has since shifted her focus, creating a new interview series called "The Originals" on the Scripps Sports Network. Her first episode airs Sept. 15 at 8 p.m.

item.title: Comedian declares Jerry Seinfeld 'uncancellable' despite 'woke' anti-Israel festival boycott
item.description: Several performers pulled out of Lisbon's inaugural MEO Commedia a La Carte Fest following headliner Jerry Seinfeld's addition, citing support for the Palestinians.
item.content:encoded:
Several performers have pulled out of an international festival in Portugal headlined by comedian Jerry Seinfeld, with some citing concerns related to the Israel-Gaza conflict and others giving no public explanation.

The withdrawals come ahead of the inaugural MEO Commedia a La Carte Fest in Lisbon, scheduled for Oct. 29 to Nov. 1. While some acts left the lineup without a public explanation, others cited political differences with performers involved in the festival.

On Saturday, actress Inês Aires Pereira announced on Instagram that she was withdrawing her show Namastê from the festival lineup. In one image, Pereira wrote in Portuguese that "one of the names persistently defends ideas and acts that I consider indefensible. We cannot minimize or normalize a genocide," according to a translation by The Hollywood Reporter.

COMEDIAN DECLARES HUGH LAURIE 'CAN'T BE CANCELED' AS ACTOR COMES TO SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM'S DEFENSE

Musical comedy duo Cebola Mol also addressed their exit on Instagram, writing in a translated caption, "We will celebrate justice, freedom and joy with you on another occasion." The post included a cartoon watermelon, which is widely used as a symbol of Palestinian solidarity.

Several departing acts did not disclose their motives. High-profile performers including pop musical project Tributo Pop, comedian Pedro Tochas, the group Conjunto Cuca Monga and visual artist Vhils all withdrew from the festival lineup without publicly stating a reason.

MICHAEL RAPAPORT SLAMS 'CLOWN' MACKLEMORE FOR ANTI-ISRAEL PERFORMANCE

Seinfeld is the festival’s main headliner and has publicly supported Israel. The festival’s website still lists him as a performer. 

His support for Israel during the conflict has drawn accolades but also fierce criticism. In June, while leaving a New York Knicks game at Madison Square Garden, Seinfeld told a streamer asking for a "Free Palestine" shoutout that "it doesn’t exist."

During an event at Duke University, Seinfeld also discussed pro-Palestinian protests, saying: "Free Palestine is, to me, just — you’re free to say you don’t like Jews. Just say you don’t like Jews."

RABID ANTI-ISRAEL ACTIVISTS SET TO HIT THE STREETS TONIGHT IN MAMDANI'S MANHATTAN

"By saying ‘Free Palestine,’ you’re not admitting what you really think," he continued. "So it’s actually — compared to the Ku Klux Klan, I’m actually thinking the Klan is actually a little better here because they can come right out and say, ‘We don’t like Blacks, we don’t like Jews.’ OK, that’s honest."

Fox News Digital reached out to Seinfeld’s team but did not hear back.

Comedian and media analyst Tim Young argued that the withdrawals hurt the departing performers far more than Seinfeld, whom he called "uncancellable."

"It was a total eye-roll for me," said Young, who also serves as a Media Fellow at the Heritage Foundation and Media Editor at The Dallas Express.

"I think anybody who is a comedian, anybody who is a performer, would want to work with basically the most successful, if not one of the most successful comedians in world history at this point. The guy's a billionaire from his comedy and his writing, and I don't know why you would want to walk away from it," he added.

Young suggested the withdrawals were simply catering to their existing fan base, calling the move "a group of woke people performing for woke people."

"They know who their audience is, they're behaving the way that their audience would behave, and just playing into it," he said, adding that the performers are likely getting more publicity from pulling out than they would have from performing.

Young doesn't believe the withdrawals will have any lasting impact on Seinfeld's standing in the comedy world.

Alanis Morissette became one of music’s biggest stars with "Jagged Little Pill," but behind the blockbuster success was a frightening wave of hostility that she says included websites plotting her murder.

Morissette, who skyrocketed to fame after the release of her 1995 album, opened up on the "Call Her Daddy" podcast about the hostility she faced at the time, including death threats and attacks from some fellow musicians.

"There was terror and resistance, but that's just normal," the singer recalled of the response she received from her lead single "You Oughta Know."

SHANIA TWAIN CONFRONTS LONGSTANDING NARRATIVE THAT HER MUSIC PROMOTES MAN-HATING

"But you know, at that point, project onto me all you want," Morissette said. "Project that I'm the Antichrist. Project that I'm terrifying or ... basically too much. My whole life I've just heard that I'm too much."

But the backlash Morissette described went far beyond criticism of her music or personality. As her fame intensified, she recalled the hostility escalating to a chilling level.

"There was a lot of hate," she told host Alex Cooper. "There were websites constructed to figure out how to murder me most elegantly.

"Well, there was a lot of hate, and it was very, very out there. And a lot of people, a lot of artists whom I respected and lived for, were disparagingly speaking about me. Later, Sinéad apologized, which was really classy. But, yeah, I mean, it was not a girl squad. There were no girl squads."

Decades later, Morissette said she views the reaction through a different lens. She compared the resentment she encountered to modern-day jealousy surrounding Taylor Swift and argued that women were often made to feel there was room for only one at the top.

You're ugly. Bye.' What? That's patriarchy. That's scarcity mindset."

Morissette started performing at a young age, including an early stint on the Canadian children’s television series "You Can’t Do That on Television." She initially found success as a dance-pop singer in Canada, but her career changed dramatically with the 1995 release of "Jagged Little Pill."

item.title: Trump administration accuses prestigious law school of favoring Black applicants over White, Asian peers
item.description: Federal officials allege a major California law school favored Black applicants over Asian and White students, but the university denies violating admissions laws.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration on Wednesday blasted the University of California, Berkeley, School of Law for allegedly favoring Black applicants while discriminating against Asian and White students, marking its latest federal action targeting race-conscious admissions policies at universities.

The Department of Justice (DOJ), along with the Department of Education, found Berkeley Law in violation of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits racial discrimination in programs and activities receiving federal funds.

"The data produced by Berkeley Law demonstrates a strong bias against Asian and White applicants, with a corresponding bias in favor of Black applicants," the DOJ said.

The findings came after officials launched a compliance review of Berkeley Law in March 2025, roughly two years after the Supreme Court struck a major blow to affirmative action programs many universities used in admissions for decades. California had already banned affirmative action in public education under Proposition 209, enacted in 1996.

JUSTICE DEPARTMENT ZEROES IN ON UCLA FOR ALLEGED ILLEGAL DEI ADMISSIONS AS ELITE SCHOOL CRACKDOWN EXPANDS

According to the DOJ's analysis, Black applicants in 2025 had "5.8 times higher odds of admission than comparable white applicants."

An analysis of LSAT scores for admitted students in 2024 and 2025 found that 37% of Black admitted applicants scored below 99% of admitted White applicants.

In addition, half of the school's admitted Black applicants had LSAT scores "below 95% of the admitted white applicants."

According to figures cited by the DOJ, median LSAT scores from 2021 through 2025 showed a persistent disparity between racial groups, with Black admits scoring around 165. Asian and White admits scored around 172, while Hispanic admits had median scores around 169.

"The median Black admit consistently has an LSAT score about 5 points lower than the median white or Asian admits," the department said in a letter to attorney Tania Faransso, who is representing the law school.

DOJ OPENS PROBE INTO PRESTIGIOUS COLLEGE OVER ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION FAVORING MINORITY STUDENTS

As of October 2025, Berkeley Law had 1,128 students enrolled. Of those, 516 were White, 293 were Asian, 51 were Black and 130 were Hispanic.

In a statement to Fox News, Berkeley Law firmly rejected the allegations, saying its admissions decisions comply with federal law and Proposition 209.

However, the school noted that the laws still allow institutions to build diverse student bodies by considering race-neutral factors, which can include socioeconomic status and personal experiences.

"Our admissions policy is clear that race is not considered in any way in admissions decisions," the school said. "Proposition 209, federal statutes and the Supreme Court’s decisions do not preclude schools from pursuing diversity so long as they give no preferences based on race. Berkeley Law does not do so."

UC Berkeley’s central administration also said the school is "committed to ensuring that every student is admitted based on their merit, and not on their race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin."

"UC Berkeley will spare no effort to provide ample evidence showing that the university complies with all relevant laws, policies and rules governing admissions," the school said.

item.title: ICE arrests Peruvian national accused of illegally voting in 2024 election as DHS cites similar cases
item.description: Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a Peruvian national, was arrested by ICE in Wichita after she allegedly voted illegally in the 2024 Kansas election.
item.content:encoded:
A Peruvian national was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after authorities say she falsely claimed to be a U.S. citizen and illegally voted in the 2024 general election in Kansas, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced Thursday.

Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a lawful permanent resident and citizen of Peru, was arrested by Homeland Security Investigations special agents after authorities determined she unlawfully voted in the Nov. 5, 2024, election in Sedgwick County, according to DHS.

The arrest comes as the Trump administration continues its crackdown on noncitizens accused of illegally voting in U.S. elections.

"This alien violated the sacred right of every American citizen," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a news release.

WATCH: ILLEGAL ALIEN BUSTED IN BATTLEGROUND STATE AFTER ALLEGEDLY COMMITTING VOTER FRAUD

"If even one noncitizen votes, that steals the voice of a U.S. citizen," Mullin continued. "Only American citizens have the right to participate in our political and election processes, and DHS will continue to investigate, seek criminal prosecution and ultimately remove aliens who vote to ensure free, fair and honest elections."

According to DHS, election records showed Dewey submitted a Kansas voter registration application and cast a provisional ballot after certifying, under penalty of perjury, that she was a U.S. citizen.

NONCITIZEN CHARGED WITH VOTING IN MINNESOTA 2024 ELECTION AFTER ADMITTING ‘MISTAKE’ TO INVESTIGATORS

During a subsequent interview with investigators, authorities said Dewey acknowledged she was a lawful permanent resident, not a U.S. citizen, and admitted voting in the 2024 general election. DHS said she later pleaded guilty to disorderly election conduct under Kansas law.

The department said Dewey was taken into ICE custody Sept. 1 after HSI agents located her at a residence in Wichita.

DHS described the arrest as the latest in the administration's effort to crack down on noncitizens accused of illegally voting in American elections.

The department pointed to several recent cases, including enforcement actions involving noncitizens from Colombia, Slovakia, Australia, Mexico and Mauritania, as well as charges against four noncitizens in New Jersey accused of illegally voting in federal elections or falsely claiming U.S. citizenship.

item.title: Trump signs act clearing the way for Medal of Honor monument on National Mall
item.description: Trump signed the act at the National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas, after meeting 15 living recipients and touring the facility.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump signed legislation Thursday authorizing the future National Medal of Honor Monument to be located within the Reserve of the National Mall in Washington, D.C., near the Lincoln Memorial, during a ceremony honoring Medal of Honor recipients in Arlington, Texas.

Trump signed the Hershel "Woody" Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act at the National Medal of Honor Museum after touring the museum and meeting more than a dozen recipients.

The legislation does not create the monument itself, which Congress previously authorized in 2021. Instead, it allows the future monument to be located within the Reserve, a protected area of the National Mall that includes some of Washington's most prominent monuments and memorials.

EXCLUSIVE: NEW AMERICA 250 MONUMENT LETS FAMILIES FIND MILITARY RELATIVES IN SECONDS: 'I HAD TEARS IN MY EYES'

Trump greeted and shook hands with recipients before taking the stage for the signing ceremony.

"We're privileged to have with us 15 of the 65 living recipients of the Congressional Medal of Honor," Trump told the audience.

"When I see the recipients of the Congressional Medal, those that are living, many are dead. They died. And they died in battle. Some of the battles are … I read inscriptions of what took place. That level of bravery is incredible," Trump said.

The act is named for Williams, a Marine who received the Medal of Honor for his actions during the Battle of Iwo Jima and was the last surviving World War II Medal of Honor recipient when he died in 2022.

HEGSETH UPGRADES ABBEY GATE MARINES' VALOR AWARDS AFTER 5-YEAR DELAY: 'THOSE DAYS ARE OVER'

Trump recounted Williams' heroism before recognizing members of his family who attended the ceremony.

"In the Battle of Iwo Jima, he carved a path to American victory, literally carved a path so soldiers could get in and win through a deadly gantlet of enemy strongholds," Trump said.

"And back and forth, he went. He just kept going back and forth," Trump continued. "And one machine gun nest after another. He knocked [them] out, and he did it for hours and hours. People said they've never seen anything quite like it."

National Medal of Honor Museum Foundation Chairman Charlotte Jones said 16 of the nation's 65 living Medal of Honor recipients were present at the museum Thursday.

SIX AMERICAN HEROES EVERYONE SHOULD KNOW THIS MEMORIAL DAY, FROM DELTA FORCE TO A WWII BOMBER CREW

"This is not a war museum. This is a museum about heart, about courage, about sacrifice and patriotism," Jones said.

The museum foundation said the effort to create and locate the monument has received eight votes in Congress over six years, all unanimously. The location act itself also passed both chambers without opposition, according to the foundation.

Jones said that bipartisan support reflected the significance of the Medal of Honor and the values associated with it.

"That is the inspirational power of the Medal of Honor," Jones said. "And that is why this project matters."

'BLACK HAWK DOWN' SNIPER SHINES LIGHT ON BRUTAL REALITY OF VIOLENT COMBAT

The future monument will be located near the Lincoln Memorial, though its precise site has not yet been selected. The National Park Service will award the specific site, after which the foundation said it will launch a design competition.

No federal funds will be used to construct the monument, according to the foundation, which will raise the money needed for the project.

Trump also reflected on the sacrifices represented by the recipients gathered for Thursday's ceremony.

9/11 MUSEUM TO OFFER FREE ADMISSION FOR VETERANS AHEAD OF MEMORIAL DAY WEEKEND

"People like this, they stood tall when their country needed heroes," Trump said.

"They carried the wounded out of battle and on their own backs and carried them back and forth," he continued. "They gave their bodies the shields for their brothers at arms. They stood in the way of bullets, purposely standing just like this and taking bullets. And it's amazing. These are amazing."

Trump said the future monument, together with the museum, would provide a permanent way to preserve those stories.

FIRST ON FOX: BEHIND THE SCENES OF ARLINGTON’S MEMORIAL DAY TRIBUTE FOR AMERICA’S 250TH BIRTHDAY

"With this museum and a new monument in Washington, D.C., America will never, ever forget what they did and what they risked and how much they risked, what they meant to their families and what they've meant to our country," Trump said.

The White House told Fox News Digital the signing was intended to recognize the recipients' service and sacrifice.

"Medal of Honor recipients represent the very best of America. President Trump honored their courage today, and a new monument will ensure the nation never forgets their valor and sacrifice," White House spokeswoman Liz Huston said.

item.title: SEN McCORMICK: The heroic passengers of Flight 93 showed America how to stand united
item.description: Todd Beamer's famous "Let's roll" rallied Flight 93 passengers to charge al Qaeda hijackers, and their six-minute fight changed the course of 9/11.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-five years ago, 40 men and women showed uncommon courage on Flight 93. Today, we honor their sacrifice and their example on a field of honor forever in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

On the morning of 9/11, I was in a skyscraper in Pittsburgh as the attacks unfolded. We knew another plane had been hijacked somewhere over Pennsylvania, but we did not know where it was or where it was headed. Then came the news from Shanksville — and, later, the story of what its passengers and crew had done.

Less than an hour after United Flight 93 left Newark, four al Qaeda terrorists seized the plane and forced the passengers and crew to the rear of the aircraft. 

Flight 93 was different from the other hijacked planes that morning because a ground delay gave its passengers time to learn of the attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. When the plane turned toward Washington, they knew that Flight 93 had become another weapon of terror.

9/11 IS BECOMING HISTORY. MY GENERATION MUST MAKE SURE AMERICA NEVER FORGETS

Through calls to loved ones and people on the ground, they learned what had happened in New York and at the Pentagon. They understood that the hijackers did not intend for them to survive and that countless more innocent lives were at stake.

C.S. Lewis wrote that courage is "the form of every virtue at the testing point." For the ordinary Americans aboard Flight 93, that testing point came without warning — and within minutes they responded in an extraordinary, distinctly American way.

They took a vote and made a plan. At 9:57 a.m., Todd Beamer, an account manager for Oracle, uttered the now-famous words, "Let’s roll," and they charged the cockpit and the knife-wielding jihadis. For six minutes, they fought to retake the plane. At 10:03, the plane flipped upside down and plowed into a farmer’s field near Shanksville. Their sacrifice denied the terrorists their target.

Twenty-five years later, their example offers lessons not only about who we were then, but also who we must continue to be.

9/11 TAUGHT US DEADLY LESSONS. 25 YEARS LATER, WE NEED A NEW MODEL TO PREVENT ATTACKS

We must remain vigilant in the face of evil. At home, that means rejecting the poisonous idea, voiced by Hasan Piker, that America "deserved 9/11." Abroad, it means taking seriously enemies who chant "Death to America" and mean it. We Americans do not go looking for a fight; but when called upon, we show the strength and courage that should make our enemies think twice. Even now, the men and women of the United States military are reminding the world that threats against America have consequences.

Vigilance must be backed by strength. When the time to act arrives, the time to prepare has passed. The passengers and crew of Flight 93 had only minutes and whatever strength they could summon. Today, advances in AI, robotics and other technologies are transforming both the threats we face and the tools we have to defeat them. America needs the strongest military in the world, equipped with the best technology and ready to give those who serve every advantage when called to fight.

Yet because evil is real, we must not blur the distinction between genuine evil and ordinary political disagreement. In those decisive minutes aboard Flight 93, no one asked who was a Republican or Democrat, where anyone came from or how anyone worshiped. They acted together as Americans. That same sense of common purpose swept the country after September 11 as strangers helped strangers, communities grieved together and a generation raised its hand to serve.

Today, that unity can seem distant. Our politics too often turns disagreement into enmity and fellow Americans into adversaries. September 11 reminds us that before we are Republicans, Independents or Democrats, we are Americans.

MIKE PENCE: THE NEXT GENERATION NEEDS FAITH IN GOD AND CONFIDENCE IN THE AMERICAN IDEAL

From Gettysburg to Normandy to Shanksville, ordinary Americans have shown the spirit, courage and character that define America at its best. President George W. Bush said the terrorists discovered that "a random group of Americans is an exceptional group of people." The passengers and crew were students and retirees, an ironworker and an attorney, business travelers and flight attendants — ordinary people who answered an extraordinary call.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

But we cannot take that spirit for granted. Only 39% of Americans say they are "extremely proud" to be American, down from 70% in 2003, and pride is even lower among younger Americans. At the same time, too many boys and young men are struggling to find purpose and a path into adulthood. Character must be taught and cultivated. We must tell these stories, call the next generation to service, and teach them that courage means self-command, responsibility and putting others before themselves.

NEW 9/11 MUSEUM EXHIBIT AIMS TO CONNECT YOUNGER AMERICANS TO THE ATTACKS THROUGH POWERFUL ARTIFACTS

That is why I encourage every American to visit the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, where I will join others in remembrance today. Bring your children and grandchildren. Stand at the crash site and listen to the calls made in the flight’s final minutes — some to say goodbye, others to explain what was happening and what they intended to do about it. You cannot hear their voices and leave unchanged.

Most of us will never face such an extraordinary test. But all of us are called, in ways large and small, to serve our country and leave it better for those who come after us.

At their testing point, the heroes of Flight 93 showed us what America still requires of you, me and each of us: the clarity to recognize evil, the strength to confront it, the unity to stand together and the courage to put country before self.

item.title: Trump faces reckoning as GOP figures label $5K promise a 'socialist vote-buying scheme'
item.description: President Donald Trump's $5,000 dividend proposal could cost over $1.2 trillion, sparking a fierce GOP debate over tariff revenue and national debt.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump’s proposal to send $5,000 checks to American adults if Republicans win both chambers of Congress is forcing Republicans to debate an idea more commonly associated with the Democratic side of the aisle: sending direct government payments to voters.

Called a "socialist vote-buying scheme" by former GOP Rep. Bob Good of Virginia, the so-called Trump Dividend would only be handed down if Republicans keep the House and Senate in November, the president announced at the party's midterm convention in Dallas.

Good warned that the checks would add to the national debt, which has topped $40 trillion.

The plan could cost more than $1.2 trillion, based on estimates of roughly 240 million eligible adults. The president cannot direct the Treasury to issue the checks without a law providing that authority, so Congress would need to authorize the spending plan.

TRUMP MAKES STUNNING FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND CASH PROMISE IN BID TO RALLY GOP VOTERS AT DALLAS MIDTERM CONVENTION

"If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them … I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000," Trump said during his keynote address Wednesday night.

He compared the payment to a cash distribution from a successful company to its shareholders and said the money would have to be spent domestically. 

"The only caveat I have is that the dividend that we're making must be spent in the United States of America," Trump said. "We don't want you going to Canada to spend the money."

"If you keep us in power and allow us to continue to do these things, then you’re going to share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we’re creating in the United States of America," Vice President JD Vance said after Trump unveiled his new idea.

Conservative commentator Matt Walsh called the plan "flagrant bribery" and said Republicans could help working Americans by allowing them to keep more of their own money through tax cuts.

"Holding it as a carrot on the stick for after the election is just shameless," Walsh wrote.

Vance and Trump both pointed to tariff revenue as a potential funding source for the payments, and questions emerged over where the money would come from to fund the dividends.

"The reason the Democrats can’t do that is because they don’t do tariffs. They don’t take in money. All they know is poverty," Trump said Wednesday night.

Treasury data show the federal government collected about $154.4 billion in customs duties from Oct. 1, 2025, through July 31, 2026, which would cover roughly 13% of the estimated $1.2 trillion cost of sending $5,000 checks to about 240 million adults.

The administration has not provided an income threshold for the proposed middle-class payments or explained how much tariff revenue would be dedicated to the program. The remaining cost would have to be covered through other federal revenue, spending reductions or additional borrowing.

CONGRESS SPENDS $7 TRILLION; HERE’S HOW THAT MATH WORKS OUT IF YOU THINK OF JUST $100

Vance also suggested in an interview after the president's speech Wednesday that the proposal could be limited to middle-class Americans rather than every adult citizen, potentially lowering the cost.

The VP defended the idea as "fundamentally a dividend for American workers," arguing that tariffs have generated revenue from foreign companies and countries that have taken advantage of American workers.

The proposal’s funding and eligibility questions have fueled criticism from fiscal conservatives, who say the plan would create a new government benefit while adding to the national debt.

Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, said the estimated $1.2 trillion cost of the dividend proposal could instead be used to eliminate taxes for married parents with dependents earning up to $200,000.

"Or maybe some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms," Roy wrote in a follow-up post.

That criticism from Republicans reflects a broader conservative argument that tax cuts are preferable to direct payments because they reduce the government’s role rather than create a new reason for Americans to rely on it.

James Fishback, a former Florida gubernatorial candidate who previously proposed a $5,000 DOGE dividend, said his plan would have returned savings generated by spending cuts. Meanwhile, he argued Trump’s proposal would add to the debt without a comparable reduction in government spending.

Investor Joe Lonsdale called the idea "bread and circus bribes." Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson urged Republican leaders to reject it and focus on reducing the debt.

Other Republicans and Trump allies are moving in the opposite direction.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said he would prepare legislation to pass the dividend after the election, while Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., asked voters how they would spend their $5,000.

The reactions show a Republican Party split between treating tariff revenue as money to return to Americans and preserving the party’s traditional emphasis on lower taxes, limited spending and less government dependence.

item.title: Trump's $5,000 dividend checks would come with a major catch under GOP senator's plan
item.description: Trump's $5,000 tariff dividend plan could cost $1.2 trillion as Sen. Bernie Moreno pushes legislation to fund checks through market access fees.
item.content:encoded:
DALLAS — There’s a push in the Senate to turn President Donald Trump’s pitch of $5,000 checks for Americans into a reality, with a couple of caveats along the way.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, plans to introduce legislation that would codify the dividend checks and wants it done as soon as the upcoming midterm elections are over, when the balance of power could tilt in favor of Democrats.

But the money, Moreno told Fox News Digital, wouldn’t come from taxpayers’ coffers. Instead, he wants to approve certain structural tariffs to act as a "market access fee" that would find its way back into the pockets of Americans.

TRUMP DEFENDS $5,000 DIVIDEND PROPOSAL, PRAISES 'BEAUTIFUL' TARIFFS ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE'

And it can only be spent in the U.S.

"This dividend would be something that is allowing working Americans to share in the prosperity of this country," Moreno said. "The money would be used only here in the United States, so it's not to be used outside the United States. I think it would provide a big economic boost to our economy."

"So, if you're a company out there, anywhere in the world, you want to sell your products in America, you either make it here in the United States, or you pay a fee to enter our market," he continued. "That money goes to funding this one-time dividend."

Trump floated the plan Wednesday night during the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas, where the GOP and several — but not all — vulnerable incumbents and candidates flocked to energize their base and pitch why they should maintain control of Congress.

TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED

The cost, however, could be an eye-popping $1.2 trillion. Moreno argued that the cost was worth it and noted that despite the steps Republicans have taken to lower costs, Americans are still feeling the crunch.

"It's about providing relief," Moreno said. "It's acknowledgment that during the Biden years, it was so bad for working families, that, despite what we've already done in 18 months, it just isn't enough to get working families to basically so that they're level, right?"

"Because they're underwater right now," he continued. "I think it's extremely important for us to understand in elected office that working families are struggling."

For the plan to work, Republicans would need to maintain their control of both chambers of Congress, and it comes as the nation’s federal deficit skyrocketed to $40 trillion last month and as the GOP has consistently pitched itself as the party of fiscal responsibility against Democrats’ wanton federal spending.

Trump's plan scored one unlikely ally in House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md., leader of a pack of fiscal hawks who routinely scoff at Congress’ inability to tackle the nation’s debt.

"Hardworking American taxpayers probably deserve a tax rebate. We're gonna have to discuss, you know, how large a rebate that would be. But I think, again, American taxpayers deserve relief from taxation. I think that's a good idea," Harris told Fox News Digital in an interview during the GOP midterm convention.

REPUBLICAN SOUNDS ALARM ON RISING DEM STAR: 'THIS GUY’S GOING TO BE A PROBLEM'

Harris said such a plan "would have to go through Congress," and he suggested that the party-line budget reconciliation process would be needed to skirt Democratic opposition.

The Senate’s top Republican agreed with Harris.

"It smells very much like a reconciliation issue," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Fox News Digital.

Thune said Senate Republicans would be willing to work with Trump and his team to get the dividends done, but noted that until Wednesday night it was a proposal that "we hadn’t heard before." He argued that the idea showed the difference between the GOP and Democrats seeking power.

"I think it illustrates the clear contrast between us and the Democrats about how you want to, how you see government functioning," Thune said. "And one is in giving more power, control, money in the pockets of the American people, and the other, giving more power to, you know, for people in Washington to tell you how to run your life."

And Republicans will likely have to rely on reconciliation to do it, given that Democrats are already slamming the idea.

"Donald Trump is a known liar. This is the biggest liar to ever serve in government, period. And look, the dividend is not happening," Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., told Fox News Digital. "He promised a dividend on tariffs, that didn't happen. He promised a dividend on Doge, that didn't happen. He promised some strange new dividend from Air Force One, what, six months ago. That never happened."

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., recoiled and slammed the move as emblematic of Trump’s presidency being "so failed and broken, he is resorting to trying to bribe the American people for their votes."

"An insult to Americans, to democracy, and an admission of how absolutely screwed he is," Schumer said on X.

Moreno countered that when it comes to dumping tens of billions of dollars outside the U.S., Democrats were all on board but didn’t show the same vigor when it came to seeing money flow back into America.

"So look, at the end of the day, these politicians are all hypocritical. They love helping anybody on earth except for working Americans," Moreno said. "They love giving money to foreign countries. They love funding endless wars. They love having us solve the entirety of the world's problems. When it comes to helping working Americans, all of a sudden, there's no money. What we're saying is no."

item.title: Hillary Clinton: 'I hate' Trump and Netanyahu's governments but love America and Israel
item.description: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton told "Morning Joe" she hates the policies of President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu but loves Israel and America.
item.content:encoded:
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said she hated the governments and policies of President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu but said she loved America and Israel during an interview Thursday.

"I have said repeatedly I love Israel and I hate Netanyahu’s government and his policies. I love America, and I hate Trump’s government and policies. I think it’s bad, in the first case for Israel, what’s happening, and I think it’s really bad for the United States, what’s happening," Clinton told MS NOW's "Morning Joe."

Clinton spoke to the MS NOW panel about Israel and achieving peace in the Middle East.

HILLARY CLINTON BREAKS WITH DEMOCRATIC CRITICS BY BACKING TRUMP’S GAZA PLAN AS THE 'ONLY GAME IN TOWN'

"I think we’ve got to be very clear, the messages we send, hopefully the Israeli people, especially after this bombshell that came out in the Israeli press, where Netanyahu had been literally called by Sheikh Mohammed, MBZ, from UAE, and warned that Hamas was planning something," Clinton said. 

"And either he didn’t believe it or he, it’s horrible to say, he wanted to see what they could plan so that then he could come down hard, and it would enhance his position."

"I don’t know what his thinking was, but the bottom line, talk about a failure of imagination. This was a failure of leadership," she continued. "This was a failure of protecting the people of Israel. He’s been told what was going to happen. So, if the Israelis want to vote for that again, then I think the United States has to take a very tough position."

"President Trump has a strong relationship with Prime Minister Netanyahu, and Israel has always been a great ally to the United States. The Israel Defense Forces were incredible partners throughout Operation Epic Fury, which decimated the Iranian regime’s military capabilities in 38 short days," a White House official told Fox News Digital.

Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed warned Netanyahu 10 days before the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks that the terrorist group was planning a major offensive. Netanyahu's office has denied the report.

"The press reports are false. No warning was given to the Prime Minister from the United Arab Emirates before October 7th. If there was any relevant information, it was passed through intelligence channels between the two countries," the prime minister's office posted to X.

Netanyahu's office did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

MASKED ISRAELI SETTLERS ATTACK NBC NEWS CREW AND PALESTINIAN FAMILY IN WEST BANK

Clinton told MS NOW she thinks the U.S. could work with a new government in Israel.

"I would hope that a new prime minister would crack down on settler violence in the West Bank," she said. "There should be no impunity for that kind of violence. It is not just about the death and destruction of the Palestinians, their property and all the rest of it. Anytime you let people have that level of violence in a society that you don’t stop, that creeps into the whole society."

"So, it’s unfair, bad and wrong for the Palestinians," Clinton added. "And it’s also very dangerous to Israel. So, yeah, I think let’s see what they vote for and see whether we can’t, you know, figure out how to have a new approach with a new government."

Clinton also spoke on the rise of socialism in the Democratic Party, and said, "Let people defend the positions they’ve taken. And I think that would be good for the Democratic Party. It would be good for the country.

VAN JONES WARNS FAR-LEFT SOCIALIST AGENDA IS 'REGRESSIVE' THREAT TO DEMOCRATIC PARTY

"Let them get out of the sloganeering and into the legislating and results-oriented impact."

item.title: Family of 9/11 hero to retrace his steps in final Tunnel to Towers stop
item.description: Frank Siller and family will retrace Stephen Siller's iconic run through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel to the Twin Towers on the 25th anniversary.
item.content:encoded:
The family of 9/11 hero Stephen Siller will mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks by retracing the FDNY firefighter's steps as he ran through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel toward the World Trade Center.

Frank Siller and other members of the Siller family will participate in the private walk before joining hundreds of friends and supporters at the FDNY Ten House.

The event will conclude the Tunnel to Towers "Steel Across America" tour, which has traveled since May bringing Siller's story and a 21-foot steel beam from the South Tower all across the nation.

FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE

On the morning of 9/11, Siller had just concluded his shift with the fire department when he received word that a plane had struck the World Trade Center.

"Stephen drove his truck to the entrance of the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, but it had already been closed for security purposes. Determined to carry out his duty, he strapped 60 lbs. of gear to his back, and raced on foot through the tunnel to the Twin Towers, where he gave up his life while saving others," the tour's website recounts.

NEW YORK JETS OWNER WOODY JOHNSON TO BE HONORED AT TUNNEL TO TOWERS GALA FOR DECADE-LONG PARTNERSHIP

Since its founding, inspired by Siller and his favorite quote, "While we have time, let us do good," Tunnel to Towers has provided more than 1,700 mortgage-free homes to the families of fallen service members and first responders, as well as to disabled veterans and first responders. The organization has also delivered housing assistance and support services to more than 20,000 homeless veterans and holds hundreds of events nationwide to honor America’s heroes and preserve the memory of those who lost their lives for future generations.

The Tunnel to Towers 9/11 Institute has helped to educate students from kindergarten through 12th grade on the "extraordinary heroism and goodness of everyday people" on Sept. 11, "while demonstrating the strength and resilience of America’s spirit." Its mobile 9/11 exhibit has traveled to nearly all 50 states as well as Canada.

To mark the 25th anniversary, Tunnel to Towers also launched its 343 Homes Initiative this year to honor the 343 New York firefighters who died on Sept. 11. According to the group, this initiative will deliver 343 mortgage-free homes to the families of fallen service members and fallen first responders as well as to catastrophically injured service members across the country.

Fox News' Peter Pinedo contributed to this report.
